solutions.text: Phần A

1. This laboratory has just installed cutting-edge scanning equipment available anywhere in the world. --- CUTTING-EDGE (adjective) = tiên tiến nhất, dẫn đầu công nghệ; luôn viết có gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ, ví dụ "cutting-edge technology/research".

2. Many household appliances become obsolete within a few years because newer models replace them. --- OBSOLETE (adjective) = lỗi thời, không còn được sản xuất/sử dụng; collocation thường gặp: "become obsolete", "render sth obsolete".

3. Smartphones have become so ubiquitous that they are found in every country and every social class. --- UBIQUITOUS (adjective) = hiện diện khắp nơi, phổ biến ở mọi nơi; cấu trúc quen thuộc "so ubiquitous as to be...", trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai /juːˈbɪk.wə.təs/.

4. Rural households without a stable internet connection are on the wrong side of a widening digital divide. --- DIGITAL DIVIDE (noun phrase) = khoảng cách số giữa nhóm có và không có khả năng tiếp cận công nghệ; collocation: "bridge/widen/close the digital divide".

5. Many citizens feel uneasy about living under constant digital surveillance. --- SURVEILLANCE (noun) = sự giám sát liên tục, có hệ thống; collocation phổ biến: "digital/mass surveillance", "under surveillance"; chú ý chính tả "ei" không phải "ai".

6. False stories designed to mislead voters spread across social media faster than fact-checkers can combat the disinformation. --- DISINFORMATION (noun) = thông tin sai lệch được lan truyền có chủ đích nhằm đánh lừa; phân biệt với "misinformation" (sai lệch không cố ý); collocation: "spread/combat disinformation".

7. The anonymity of the internet sometimes encourages people to post cruel or reckless comments. --- ANONYMITY (noun) = sự ẩn danh, tình trạng không bị nhận diện; collocation: "online anonymity", "a cloak of anonymity"; trọng âm rơi vào "nym".

8. Messaging apps rely on strong encryption so that no third party can read the content of any conversation. --- ENCRYPTION (noun) = quá trình mã hoá dữ liệu để ngăn truy cập trái phép; collocation: "end-to-end encryption", "data encryption"; đối lập là "decryption".

9. The company admitted that hackers had caused a massive data breach affecting millions of customers' personal records. --- DATA BREACH (noun phrase) = vụ vi phạm/rò rỉ dữ liệu do truy cập trái phép; collocation: "suffer/prevent a data breach"; "breach" phát âm /briːtʃ/.

10. Some teenagers are victims of repeated cyberbullying from classmates, which can seriously damage their mental health. --- CYBERBULLYING (noun) = hành vi bắt nạt qua các phương tiện điện tử; collocation: "tackle cyberbullying", "a victim of cyberbullying".

11. Businesses that fail to adopt cloud computing risk falling seriously behind the curve compared with their competitors. --- BEHIND THE CURVE (idiom) = tụt hậu, không bắt kịp xu hướng mới; đối lập là "ahead of the curve"; thường đi với "fall/seriously behind the curve".

12. After years of financial losses, the board finally decided to pull the plug on the app permanently. --- PULL THE PLUG (ON STH) (idiom) = đột ngột ngừng hỗ trợ/cấp vốn cho một dự án khiến nó chấm dứt; luôn cần giới từ "on" trước đối tượng bị dừng.
Phần B

1. Band 6: People use their phones too much and it is bad for them. Band 7: Many people spend far too much time on their phones, which can have a negative effect on their concentration and relationships. Band 8: An over-dependence on smartphones is increasingly eroding attention spans and undermining the quality of face-to-face communication.

2. Band 6: The internet has made it easy for young people to learn new things. Band 7: The internet has given young people much easier access to information, allowing them to pick up new skills more quickly than before. Band 8: Ubiquitous internet access has democratised learning, enabling today's digital natives to acquire cutting-edge skills far more rapidly than previous generations ever could.

3. Band 6: Some people say social media is bad for teenagers' mental health. Band 7: Many experts believe that spending too long on social media can damage teenagers' mental health and self-esteem. Band 8: A growing body of research links prolonged social media use among adolescents to measurable declines in mental well-being, particularly through algorithmically reinforced echo chambers.

4. Band 6: Governments should make rules to stop big companies doing whatever they want. Band 7: Governments need to introduce stricter regulations to prevent large tech companies from abusing their power. Band 8: Given the scale at which dominant platforms now operate, governments must impose robust regulatory frameworks to curb unchecked algorithmic governance and corporate overreach.

5. Band 6: Old people sometimes find it hard to use new technology. Band 7: Older generations often struggle to keep up with rapidly changing technology, unlike younger, more tech-savvy users. Band 8: Many older adults find themselves falling behind the curve as digital innovation accelerates, widening the generational digital divide.

6. Band 6: It is important to keep your personal information safe online. Band 7: It is essential to protect your personal data online, for example by using strong passwords and secure websites. Band 8: Safeguarding personal data has become imperative in an era of pervasive surveillance, making practices such as end-to-end encryption indispensable rather than optional.

7. Band 6: Working from home is possible now because of better technology. Band 7: Improvements in technology have made it much easier for employees to work remotely from home. Band 8: Advances in connectivity and collaborative software have rendered remote working not merely feasible but, for many organisations, the default mode of operation.

8. Band 6: Robots and computers will probably take over many jobs in the future. Band 7: In the future, many jobs are likely to be replaced by robots and computer programs. Band 8: As artificial intelligence continues to mature, a substantial proportion of routine occupations are likely to become obsolete, displaced by increasingly autonomous systems.

passages.text: In its earliest formulation, the digital divide was a question about hardware. Researchers, ministries and donor agencies in the 1990s catalogued the gap between households with computers and those without, and between countries with broadband infrastructure and those still relying on slow dial-up connections. The implicit assumption was that, once devices and bandwidth had been distributed, the divide would close of its own accord. Two decades of empirical work have made that assumption increasingly difficult to defend. As the sociologist Eszter Hargittai of the University of Zurich has put it, the more carefully one measures, the more layered the divide turns out to be: a gap in equipment is followed by a gap in skills, a gap in skills by a gap in autonomy, and a gap in autonomy by a gap in tangible benefits. Each layer is real, and each requires a different kind of policy response.

What the Hargittai-style research programme has documented is that the second-level divide — the gap in digital skills — does not vanish simply because devices become cheaper. Survey work in Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom has consistently found that older adults, less educated workers and recent migrants score lower on practical skills tasks even when controlling for time spent online. The professor Alexander van Deursen of the University of Twente has argued that, in some respects, the skill gap has widened as platforms have become more sophisticated: the gap between casual scrolling and effective use of public-service portals, employment search engines or banking interfaces grows with each successive interface redesign.

A third, more recent line of work has shifted the unit of analysis from individuals to the digital architectures in which they operate. The legal scholar Frank Pasquale, formerly of the University of Maryland, has argued that the central question is no longer who can log on but who controls the rules of the platforms once they have. Pasquale's notion of the "black box society" describes systems in which the criteria for ranking content, allocating gigs or assessing credit are opaque to the users they govern. From this vantage, the digital divide is partly redefined as an information asymmetry: a small number of platform operators understand the system fully, the rest navigate by trial and error.

The sociology of platform work has developed in parallel. Drawing on interviews and observational studies, Juliet Schor of Boston College has analysed the experiences of workers on labour platforms such as those operating ride-hailing, food delivery and short-term home rentals. Her central finding is that the platforms produce a characteristic mixture of formal autonomy and effective control: workers nominally choose their hours, yet the platform's rating system, dispatch algorithm and pricing dynamics shape behaviour as tightly as a conventional employment contract. Schor distinguishes between workers who use platform earnings to supplement other income, for whom the flexibility is genuinely valuable, and those who depend on platform work as their primary livelihood, for whom the same flexibility translates into a form of precariousness.

These three positions are not in direct opposition, but they pull policy in different directions. If the priority is access, the appropriate response is infrastructure investment and digital-skills training. If the priority is platform governance, the focus shifts to algorithmic transparency, audit rights and external oversight of ranking systems. If the priority is the quality of platform work, the policy instruments come from labour law: portable benefits, minimum-rate floors and access to collective representation. The disagreement is, at root, about which level of the system is doing the most work in shaping outcomes.

Empirical comparisons across jurisdictions have begun to clarify, if not to settle, that question. A 2022 review of ride-hailing regulation in fifteen cities, conducted at the Oxford Internet Institute, found that minimum-rate floors and transparency requirements appear to raise driver earnings without obviously reducing service availability, although the size of the effect varies considerably with local labour-market conditions. Whether the same balance holds in food delivery, where margins are thinner and incumbents financially weaker, remains, in the institute's careful phrasing, an open question.

Defenders of a more market-led settlement push back along several lines. Platform operators argue that opacity is partly a function of competitive advantage: publishing the inner workings of a ranking system invites gaming and degrades the experience for all users. Some economists, particularly those working in the tradition of innovation studies, have warned that heavy-handed transparency requirements can lock in current incumbents at the expense of newer entrants whose interfaces are still evolving. None of this disposes of the original concern about asymmetry, but it does suggest that the trade-offs are sharper than the language of accountability sometimes implies.

Pressed on where the evidence now points, Hargittai and Pasquale would answer in different vocabularies but to much the same effect: the binary of "access" and "no access" has outlived its usefulness. Hardware and bandwidth still matter, particularly in rural regions and lower-income countries; skills and autonomy matter at every level of provision; and the architecture of platforms shapes the experience of users and workers however cheaply the underlying devices have been distributed. The live question, both have observed, is no longer whether a person is connected but on what terms that connection is granted.

The next layer is already arriving. Generative AI systems are adding fresh gaps in skills, autonomy and benefit that show up in early survey data before the previous gaps have closed. On the pattern of the past two decades, the safest planning assumption is that the divide will keep reshaping itself faster than any single regulatory cycle, so that the policy instruments most likely to remain useful are those flexible enough to be redirected as the architecture changes. The next divide, in short, rarely waits for the previous one to be solved.

audio_scripts.text: Right, settle in. Today's tutorial — we've got Hae-Jin and Bilal reporting on their digital-inclusion fieldwork. Hae-Jin, you wanna kick us off? And for the recording, could you spell your surname?

Sure. Hae-Jin Roh — that's R-O-H, just three letters, no W, no silent letters. People sometimes write it as R-O-W or R-O-H-E; mine is plain R-O-H. My project surveyed seventy-two rural-broadband households across the Northvale catchment region. (Q1)

Erm, the baseline survey ran in 2020 — sorry, no, 2019 — and the follow-up wave closed in 2023. So roughly four years end to end. Originally we'd planned to wrap up in 2022, but lockdown effects, you know, pushed everything back by twelve months. (Q2)
Okay. Just to clarify tense-wise for the recording — your follow-up FINISHED in 2023, the journal paper goes out this year, correct?
Right. Paper 2026, but the longitudinal extension we're gonna run begins in 2028.

Well, the dominant theoretical lens is what Jan van Dijk called the "second-level digital divide framework". And just to flag the terminology — you'll see related labels in the older literature: access gap, connectivity inequality, infrastructure asymmetry. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena. The current scholarly term, though, is second-level digital divide. I'll stick with that. (Q3)

Yeah, and I'm gonna echo Hae-Jin's framing. In my sample — fifty-three remote-worker households across rural Manitoba — most respondents said high-speed connectivity meaningfully reshaped their daily routines. Actually, sorry, let me be precise — thirty-nine out of fifty-three, so roughly seventy-four per cent. Only a few — about thirteen per cent — described connectivity as marginal to their routines, and some — thirteen per cent again — reported neutral effects. (Q4)
Right. Now, Hae-Jin, did your sample confirm the "infrastructure-solves-the-divide" thesis?

Sorta, yeah, but with caveats. Most of the households I surveyed did NOT regard physical broadband infrastructure as the principal barrier. The salient gap, well, was skills literacy — the capacity to use the connection productively. Only a small minority — fewer than fifteen per cent — cited bandwidth itself as the deciding factor. (Q5)

And, kinda interesting on the device axis — so-called multi-device saturation, where households juggle four or more concurrent connected devices per person, that's actually rising sharply in higher-income suburbs. The literature suggests this complicates rather than alleviates effective use.
Hmm. Hae-Jin, did you stratify by income decile?
We did. Counter-intuitively, the LOWEST income decile reported the highest perceived benefit from new broadband, not the top.
Well, it's about counterfactual contrast — low-income households previously had near-zero connectivity, so even modest provision is transformative.

And one final point — generational variance. In multigenerational households with grandparents present, digital-skill transfer across generations was, um, considerably stronger than in nuclear households. Researchers attribute it to shared screen-time as a teaching context.

Right. Now, going back to what Hae-Jin mentioned at the start — that "current scholarly term" — that's the construct we'll operationalise next week. Oh, and Bilal, on your seventy-four-per-cent figure: the implication that connectivity reshapes routines aligns with van Dijk, but Hae-Jin's skills-literacy finding qualifies it. Good tension. Thanks both. (Q6)

blocks.text: Whether digital technology widens the gaps between social groups or helps to close them is one of the defining debates of our era. While techno-optimists point to unprecedented access to information and markets, critics highlight a deepening digital divide. In my view, technology is neither inherently equalising nor inherently divisive; its effects depend heavily on the policies that govern its use.

Those who argue that technology closes gaps usually emphasise frictionless connectivity. With a smartphone and an internet connection, a farmer in a remote village can now check market prices, take online courses and reach customers worldwide. It is this democratising effect that has, in many regions, allowed previously marginalised groups - women, rural youth, micro-entrepreneurs - to bypass traditional gatekeepers. Mobile banking, in particular, has brought millions of previously unbanked citizens into the formal economy.

On the other hand, critics argue, with some force, that the benefits of digitalisation accrue disproportionately to those who are already tech-savvy and well-resourced. Digital natives raised in affluent households acquire cutting-edge skills early, while children without reliable internet or modern devices fall further behind. Furthermore, automation tends to displace routine workers while rewarding capital owners, widening the income gap, and algorithmic curation can entrench political divisions.

In my view, technology is best understood as a force multiplier whose impact depends on regulation, education and infrastructure. Provided that governments invest in digital literacy, affordable connectivity and meaningful reskilling, the gap may eventually narrow. Without such interventions, however, the digital revolution will likely deepen the divide between those equipped with powerful tools and those left behind.

Whether digital technology compresses or aggravates social inequality is among the most consequential debates of our generation. Optimists invoke unprecedented connectivity; sceptics point to a widening digital divide and the polarising logic of algorithmic curation. My own position is that, absent deliberate policy intervention, technology tends to amplify pre-existing inequalities, even though it harbours genuine equalising potential.

Defenders of the optimistic view marshal compelling evidence. Mobile penetration has, in many emerging economies, leapfrogged legacy infrastructure, granting smallholders, micro-entrepreneurs and rural women access to markets, finance and education at little marginal cost. So transformative has this shift been that fintech platforms now serve hundreds of millions of previously unbanked citizens, while open-courseware portals offer elite instruction free of charge. Such democratisation of knowledge, they argue, dissolves geographic and class barriers that earlier media never could.

The counter-position, however, deserves equal weight. Critics observe that the gains of digitalisation accrue disproportionately to digital natives in affluent households, while families without reliable broadband fall steadily behind - a stratification reinforced by automation, which displaces routine labour while inflating the returns to capital and high-skilled cognition. Furthermore, algorithmic curation increasingly mediates access to jobs, credit and information, embedding historic biases under a veneer of objectivity. Were these dynamics left unchecked, platform monopolies would entrench, rather than dissolve, structural disadvantage.

In my view, technology is best understood as a force multiplier whose distributional effects hinge on regulation, education and infrastructure. Provided that states invest meaningfully in digital literacy, universal connectivity and reskilling - and that platform power is subjected to credible oversight - the gap may narrow. Otherwise, the digital revolution risks consolidating a two-tier society in which connectivity itself becomes the new caste marker.

solutions.text: Phần A

1. This laboratory has just installed cutting-edge scanning equipment available anywhere in the world. --- CUTTING-EDGE (adjective) = tiên tiến nhất, dẫn đầu công nghệ; luôn viết có gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ, ví dụ "cutting-edge technology/research".

2. Many household appliances become obsolete within a few years because newer models replace them. --- OBSOLETE (adjective) = lỗi thời, không còn được sản xuất/sử dụng; collocation thường gặp: "become obsolete", "render sth obsolete".

3. Smartphones have become so ubiquitous that they are found in every country and every social class. --- UBIQUITOUS (adjective) = hiện diện khắp nơi, phổ biến ở mọi nơi; cấu trúc quen thuộc "so ubiquitous as to be...", trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai /juːˈbɪk.wə.təs/.

4. Rural households without a stable internet connection are on the wrong side of a widening digital divide. --- DIGITAL DIVIDE (noun phrase) = khoảng cách số giữa nhóm có và không có khả năng tiếp cận công nghệ; collocation: "bridge/widen/close the digital divide".

5. Many citizens feel uneasy about living under constant digital surveillance. --- SURVEILLANCE (noun) = sự giám sát liên tục, có hệ thống; collocation phổ biến: "digital/mass surveillance", "under surveillance"; chú ý chính tả "ei" không phải "ai".

6. False stories designed to mislead voters spread across social media faster than fact-checkers can combat the disinformation. --- DISINFORMATION (noun) = thông tin sai lệch được lan truyền có chủ đích nhằm đánh lừa; phân biệt với "misinformation" (sai lệch không cố ý); collocation: "spread/combat disinformation".

7. The anonymity of the internet sometimes encourages people to post cruel or reckless comments. --- ANONYMITY (noun) = sự ẩn danh, tình trạng không bị nhận diện; collocation: "online anonymity", "a cloak of anonymity"; trọng âm rơi vào "nym".

8. Messaging apps rely on strong encryption so that no third party can read the content of any conversation. --- ENCRYPTION (noun) = quá trình mã hoá dữ liệu để ngăn truy cập trái phép; collocation: "end-to-end encryption", "data encryption"; đối lập là "decryption".

9. The company admitted that hackers had caused a massive data breach affecting millions of customers' personal records. --- DATA BREACH (noun phrase) = vụ vi phạm/rò rỉ dữ liệu do truy cập trái phép; collocation: "suffer/prevent a data breach"; "breach" phát âm /briːtʃ/.

10. Some teenagers are victims of repeated cyberbullying from classmates, which can seriously damage their mental health. --- CYBERBULLYING (noun) = hành vi bắt nạt qua các phương tiện điện tử; collocation: "tackle cyberbullying", "a victim of cyberbullying".

11. Businesses that fail to adopt cloud computing risk falling seriously behind the curve compared with their competitors. --- BEHIND THE CURVE (idiom) = tụt hậu, không bắt kịp xu hướng mới; đối lập là "ahead of the curve"; thường đi với "fall/seriously behind the curve".

12. After years of financial losses, the board finally decided to pull the plug on the app permanently. --- PULL THE PLUG (ON STH) (idiom) = đột ngột ngừng hỗ trợ/cấp vốn cho một dự án khiến nó chấm dứt; luôn cần giới từ "on" trước đối tượng bị dừng.
Phần B

1. Band 6: People use their phones too much and it is bad for them. Band 7: Many people spend far too much time on their phones, which can have a negative effect on their concentration and relationships. Band 8: An over-dependence on smartphones is increasingly eroding attention spans and undermining the quality of face-to-face communication.

2. Band 6: The internet has made it easy for young people to learn new things. Band 7: The internet has given young people much easier access to information, allowing them to pick up new skills more quickly than before. Band 8: Ubiquitous internet access has democratised learning, enabling today's digital natives to acquire cutting-edge skills far more rapidly than previous generations ever could.

3. Band 6: Some people say social media is bad for teenagers' mental health. Band 7: Many experts believe that spending too long on social media can damage teenagers' mental health and self-esteem. Band 8: A growing body of research links prolonged social media use among adolescents to measurable declines in mental well-being, particularly through algorithmically reinforced echo chambers.

4. Band 6: Governments should make rules to stop big companies doing whatever they want. Band 7: Governments need to introduce stricter regulations to prevent large tech companies from abusing their power. Band 8: Given the scale at which dominant platforms now operate, governments must impose robust regulatory frameworks to curb unchecked algorithmic governance and corporate overreach.

5. Band 6: Old people sometimes find it hard to use new technology. Band 7: Older generations often struggle to keep up with rapidly changing technology, unlike younger, more tech-savvy users. Band 8: Many older adults find themselves falling behind the curve as digital innovation accelerates, widening the generational digital divide.

6. Band 6: It is important to keep your personal information safe online. Band 7: It is essential to protect your personal data online, for example by using strong passwords and secure websites. Band 8: Safeguarding personal data has become imperative in an era of pervasive surveillance, making practices such as end-to-end encryption indispensable rather than optional.

7. Band 6: Working from home is possible now because of better technology. Band 7: Improvements in technology have made it much easier for employees to work remotely from home. Band 8: Advances in connectivity and collaborative software have rendered remote working not merely feasible but, for many organisations, the default mode of operation.

8. Band 6: Robots and computers will probably take over many jobs in the future. Band 7: In the future, many jobs are likely to be replaced by robots and computer programs. Band 8: As artificial intelligence continues to mature, a substantial proportion of routine occupations are likely to become obsolete, displaced by increasingly autonomous systems.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)

The Automation of Labour: Studies suggest that AI and automation will displace millions of routine manual and administrative jobs, but will also create new roles requiring advanced digital literacy and reskilling.
The Attention Economy: Social media algorithms are deliberately designed to maximise user engagement, essentially turning human attention into a monetized product for advertisers.

Data as the New Oil: Tech giants harvest enormous amounts of user data (digital footprints) to train AI models and deliver hyper-targeted advertisements, raising unprecedented ethical and privacy concerns.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Does Technology Connect or Isolate Us?

Connects Us (Pros): Overcomes geographical barriers, allowing frictionless communication via instant messaging and video calls; creates global communities for people with niche interests who might feel alone locally.

Isolates Us (Cons): Superficial online interactions replace deep, meaningful face-to-face relationships; people become glued to their screens in public spaces, leading to social alienation; creates echo chambers that divide society politically.
Topic: Artificial Intelligence (Utopia or Dystopia?)

Utopia (Benefits): AI algorithms can analyse medical data faster than human doctors to diagnose diseases; automation takes over dangerous or monotonous tasks, freeing humans to focus on creative and strategic pursuits.

Dystopia (Risks): Mass unemployment for blue-collar and even white-collar workers; algorithmic bias can lead to unfair decisions in hiring and law enforcement; the terrifying potential of autonomous weapons.
Topic: Children and Technology

Arguments for early exposure: Children are digital natives who must learn tech-savvy skills early to survive in the modern job market; interactive apps and VR offer highly immersive and effective educational experiences.
Arguments against early exposure: Excessive screen time hinders physical development and social skills; children are highly vulnerable to cyberbullying and predatory algorithms online.

Cue card: Describe a piece of technology that has changed society. You should say: what the technology is; when it became widespread; what impact it has had; and explain whether you think the change has been mostly positive or negative.
Model Answer (≈ 274 words, Band 7.5–8.0):

The technology I'd single out as genuinely civilisation-altering is the smartphone — specifically the post-iPhone touchscreen paradigm that crystallised around 2007 and achieved near-universal penetration within a decade. What makes the smartphone uniquely transformative, in my view, is that it collapsed previously distinct technologies — the camera, GPS, payment terminal, library, broadcast medium and social platform — into a single pocket-sized device, fundamentally restructuring how humans access information, transact and relate to one another.

Its diffusion was extraordinarily rapid. By 2023, global smartphone penetration had surpassed 6.9 billion devices, meaning roughly 86% of adults worldwide now carry one. In Vietnam, mobile commerce alone accounts for over 60% of e-commerce transactions, a shift that would have been unthinkable fifteen years ago.

The societal impact is, I think, genuinely double-edged. On the positive side of the ledger, smartphones have democratised access to education, banking and healthcare in ways that meaningfully reduced the urban-rural digital divide. Telemedicine apps now reach remote villages; mobile-money platforms like Vietnam's MoMo have brought millions of unbanked citizens into the formal economy. The flip side, however, is rather sobering. Algorithmic feeds engineered for maximum engagement have created echo chambers and fuelled what researchers term "continuous partial attention" — a state of perpetual distraction that, according to a growing body of research, correlates with measurable declines in adolescent mental health.

On balance, I'd judge the change as net positive, though only marginally so. The productivity gains and connective potential are enormous, but they have been substantially offset by the attention-economy externalities of surveillance capitalism. Whether this calculus improves hinges critically on whether we develop the regulatory architecture to rein in the worst excesses.

sections.title: PART 2 — Describe a piece of technology that has changed society

blocks.text: Q1: Has social media been a net positive for society?

Honestly, I find myself increasingly sceptical, though I wouldn't dismiss the upside entirely. On the credit side, platforms have democratised voice — the Arab Spring, #MeToo and countless grassroots fundraising campaigns would scarcely have been possible without them. They've also enabled diasporic communities to maintain meaningful ties across continents. That said, the structural design of these platforms — engagement-maximising algorithms that systematically privilege outrage over nuance — has corroded public discourse in measurable ways. Research on algorithmically curated content has found that exposure to it correlates with a measurable increase in affective polarisation. What really tips my judgement towards the negative is the documented impact on adolescent mental health, particularly among teenage girls, where rates of anxiety and self-harm have surged in lockstep with smartphone adoption. So while social media is not inherently malign, the current business model has produced an extractive ecosystem that I think requires fundamental redesign.
Q2: Should governments regulate big tech companies more strictly?

Emphatically yes, and the regulatory lag is already costing us dearly. Tech giants operate at a scale and pace that classical antitrust frameworks, designed for industrial-era monopolies, simply cannot accommodate. The EU's Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act, which came into full force in 2024, represent the most ambitious attempt thus far — imposing transparency obligations on algorithmic recommender systems and structural separation requirements on so-called gatekeeper platforms. What I find particularly promising about the European approach is the move towards interoperability mandates, which could meaningfully erode the network-effect moats that entrench incumbents. The counter-argument, of course, is that heavy-handed regulation could stifle innovation and entrench compliance-heavy incumbents at the expense of startups. That's a legitimate concern, but I think it's outweighed by the systemic risks of unregulated algorithmic governance — particularly around election integrity, data sovereignty and child safety online.
Q3: Will Web3 and decentralised technologies genuinely transform society?

I'm genuinely on the fence here, though leaning towards cautious skepticism. The Web3 thesis — that blockchain-based decentralisation will return data sovereignty to users — is intellectually compelling, and certain niches like cross-border remittances and supply-chain provenance have shown real product-market fit. Bitcoin remittances to El Salvador, for instance, have shaved meaningful percentages off Western Union's traditional fees. However, the broader ecosystem remains dogged by speculation, energy intensity and usability barriers that have, frankly, prevented mainstream adoption. The collapse of FTX and Terra-Luna exposed the gap between libertarian rhetoric and operational reality. What might genuinely move the needle is the gradual maturation of zero-knowledge proofs and Layer-2 scaling solutions, which could finally deliver on the privacy and throughput promises. But societal transformation? That's a tall order — I'd give it maybe a 30% probability over the next two decades, contingent on regulatory clarity emerging.

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas (before listening)

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good afternoon. Today's lecture excavates three interlocking dynamics of contemporary technopolitics: the digital divide, algorithmic governance and the platform economy. The popular framing of technology as inherently democratising, I will argue, is sociologically naive.

> Let us begin with the digital divide. The International Telecommunication Union estimates that, as of 2023, approximately two and a half billion people remain offline. Yet the contemporary scholarly consensus, advanced by the Oxford Internet Institute's Mark Graham, recognises three nested divides: the access divide, the skills divide and the outcomes divide. Mere connectivity, in other words, does not translate automatically into economic empowerment; without digital literacy and meaningful content, infrastructure alone is performative.

> Now, algorithmic governance. Decisions once entrusted to civil servants — welfare eligibility, predictive policing, child-protection risk scoring — are increasingly delegated to opaque models. The Dutch toeslagenaffaire of 2019 saw an automated fraud-detection system wrongly accuse roughly twenty-six thousand families, disproportionately those with dual nationality, of benefit fraud. The episode triggered the government's resignation. Algorithmic governance, it transpires, is governance by another name — and it must answer to due process.

> Finally, the platform economy. The MIT economist Erik Brynjolfsson has documented how network effects, switching costs and the winner-take-most dynamic produce structural concentration: five firms — Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta — accounted for nearly a quarter of the S&P 500's value by 2024. The European Union's Digital Markets Act, in force from 2024, designates "gatekeepers" and mandates interoperability, attempting to dilute that concentration.

Now, that plot of market capitalisation against enforcement actions in figure four reveals something I want to name explicitly before we interpret it — a striking lag, a structural mismatch between the velocity of platform growth and the glacial pace of regulatory response. But there is a deeper layer beneath the three dynamics I sketched, and it concerns the raw material the whole system runs on: data, and specifically whose data, extracted under what terms. [pause] Shoshana Zuboff's account of surveillance capitalism makes the case that behavioural data is harvested as a free raw input — a kind of digital enclosure of the commons of human experience — and then refined into prediction products sold to the highest bidder.

And this folds back into the divides I opened with, in a way that is easy to miss. The communities on the wrong side of the access and skills gaps are, paradoxically, often the most intensively datafied. Think of biometric ID schemes rolled out across the global South, or welfare systems that demand fingerprint verification for a food ration. [pause] Virginia Eubanks, in her fieldwork, documents precisely this — that the poor are not under-surveilled but over-surveilled, subjected to a degree of algorithmic scrutiny the affluent would never tolerate. The divide is not simply about who has access; it is about who is rendered legible, and exposed, to the system.

There is also a worrying feedback loop worth flagging. Algorithmic governance trained on historical data inherits historical bias, then operationalises it at scale, then generates new records that appear to confirm the original prejudice — a self-fulfilling statistical prophecy. The Dutch case I cited was not an aberration; it was the architecture working exactly as built. [pause] Um, that is what makes mere transparency insufficient — you can audit a system and still find it faithfully reproducing an injustice it was never told to question. Which brings us to the unavoidable governance question the final section must confront, namely whether…

> The synthesis is cautionary: technology distributes opportunity unevenly, encodes political choices, and concentrates capital. Now, please look at figure four, which plots platform market capitalisation against regulatory enforcement actions…

Dung 'Provided that' va 'otherwise' de neu dieu kien hai chieu.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~261 words)

Whether digital technology widens the gaps between social groups or helps to close them is one of the defining debates of our era. While techno-optimists point to unprecedented access to information and markets, critics highlight a deepening digital divide. In my view, technology is neither inherently equalising nor inherently divisive; its effects depend heavily on the policies that govern its use.

Those who argue that technology closes gaps usually emphasise frictionless connectivity. With a smartphone and an internet connection, a farmer in a remote village can now check market prices, take online courses and reach customers worldwide. It is this democratising effect that has, in many regions, allowed previously marginalised groups — women, rural youth, micro-entrepreneurs — to bypass traditional gatekeepers. Mobile banking, in particular, has brought millions of previously unbanked citizens into the formal economy.

On the other hand, critics argue, with some force, that the benefits of digitalisation accrue disproportionately to those who are already tech-savvy and well-resourced. Digital natives raised in affluent households acquire cutting-edge skills early, while children without reliable internet or modern devices fall further behind. Furthermore, automation tends to displace routine workers while rewarding capital owners, widening the income gap, and algorithmic curation can entrench political divisions.

In my view, technology is best understood as a force multiplier whose impact depends on regulation, education and infrastructure. Provided that governments invest in digital literacy, affordable connectivity and meaningful reskilling, the gap may eventually narrow. Without such interventions, however, the digital revolution will likely deepen the divide between those equipped with powerful tools and those left behind.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~280 words)

Whether digital technology compresses or aggravates social inequality is among the most consequential debates of our generation. Optimists invoke unprecedented connectivity; sceptics point to a widening digital divide and the polarising logic of algorithmic curation. My own position is that, absent deliberate policy intervention, technology tends to amplify pre-existing inequalities, even though it harbours genuine equalising potential.

Defenders of the optimistic view marshal compelling evidence. Mobile penetration has, in many emerging economies, leapfrogged legacy infrastructure, granting smallholders, micro-entrepreneurs and rural women access to markets, finance and education at little marginal cost. So transformative has this shift been that fintech platforms now serve hundreds of millions of previously unbanked citizens, while open-courseware portals offer elite instruction free of charge. Such democratisation of knowledge, they argue, dissolves geographic and class barriers that earlier media never could.

The counter-position, however, deserves equal weight. Critics observe that the gains of digitalisation accrue disproportionately to digital natives in affluent households, while families without reliable broadband fall steadily behind — a stratification reinforced by automation, which displaces routine labour while inflating the returns to capital and high-skilled cognition. Furthermore, algorithmic curation increasingly mediates access to jobs, credit and information, embedding historic biases under a veneer of objectivity. Were these dynamics left unchecked, platform monopolies would entrench, rather than dissolve, structural disadvantage.

In my view, technology is best understood as a force multiplier whose distributional effects hinge on regulation, education and infrastructure. Provided that states invest meaningfully in digital literacy, universal connectivity and reskilling — and that platform power is subjected to credible oversight — the gap may narrow. Otherwise, the digital revolution risks consolidating a two-tier society in which connectivity itself becomes the new caste marker.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dung cau truc cao cap xuyen suot (dao ngu 'So transformative has this shift been that...', dao ngu dieu kien 'Were these dynamics left unchecked', cleft ngam) trong khi Band 7 chi dung mot lan.

•  Band 8 thay cac cum hoi doi thuong cua Band 7 ('tech-savvy and well-resourced', 'fall further behind') bang nominalisation va lexis Band 8 ('stratification', 'distributional effects', 'a veneer of objectivity', 'caste marker').
•  Band 8 co lap truong sac hon va cohesion muot hon ('The counter-position, however, deserves equal weight'; 'Provided that... — and that...'), nang Task Response va Coherence len mot bac ro ret.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khả năng hoặc tình trạng kết nối, đặc biệt trong công nghệ và viễn thông.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We live in an age of hyper-**connectivity**, where the internet lets us communicate with anyone, anywhere, at the click of a button.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
connect (kết nối) + -ivity (tính chất) → connectivity = khả năng kết nối.
vocabulary.common_error: *Connectivity* thường là danh từ không đếm được; không dùng *connectivity* khi chỉ muốn nói một mối quan hệ xã hội (*connection*).
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of being connected to other things, especially devices or networks, or the ability to make such connections
vocabulary.definition_vi: khả năng/tình trạng kết nối (đặc biệt trong công nghệ, viễn thông)
vocabulary.example: We live in an age of hyper-connectivity, where the internet lets us communicate with anyone, anywhere, at the click of a button.
vocabulary.memory_hook: connect (kết nối) + -ivity (tính chất) → connectivity = khả năng kết nối.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thế hệ lớn lên cùng công nghệ số từ nhỏ nên rất thành thạo và tự nhiên khi sử dụng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Digital natives** raised in affluent households acquire cutting-edge skills early, while children without reliable internet fall further behind.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
native (người bản xứ) → sinh ra đã sống trong thế giới số → digital native.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Digital natives' luôn ở số nhiều và không thêm 's' vào 'digital'; đối lập là 'digital immigrants', không phải 'digital foreigners'.
vocabulary.definition_en: people who have grown up using digital technology from a very young age and are therefore very comfortable with it
vocabulary.definition_vi: thế hệ thành thạo công nghệ số từ nhỏ
vocabulary.example: Digital natives raised in affluent households acquire cutting-edge skills early, while children without reliable internet fall further behind.
vocabulary.memory_hook: native (người bản xứ) → sinh ra đã sống trong thế giới số → digital native.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Dấu vết dữ liệu mà một người để lại khi hoạt động trên internet.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Be careful about what you post online so you don't leave a negative **digital footprint**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
footprint (dấu chân) để lại trên cát → trên mạng cũng để lại "dấu chân số".
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *leave/create/manage a digital footprint*; không hiểu là một tệp duy nhất vì đây là toàn bộ dấu vết dữ liệu trực tuyến.
vocabulary.definition_en: the unique trail of data that a person leaves behind while using the internet
vocabulary.definition_vi: dấu vết kỹ thuật số (dữ liệu để lại khi dùng internet)
vocabulary.example: Be careful about what you post online so you don't leave a negative digital footprint.
vocabulary.memory_hook: footprint (dấu chân) để lại trên cát → trên mạng cũng để lại 'dấu chân số'.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vụ việc dữ liệu nhạy cảm bị truy cập hoặc tiết lộ trái phép.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> As we share more online, the risk of a massive **data breach** grows exponentially.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
breach = lỗ hổng/vi phạm → "data breach" = lỗ hổng khiến dữ liệu bị lộ.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Breach' phát âm là /briːtʃ/ (giống 'beach'), không phải /breɪtʃ/; đừng nhầm với 'breech' (mông, phần đuôi súng).
vocabulary.definition_en: an incident in which sensitive or confidential data is accessed or released without authorisation
vocabulary.definition_vi: vụ vi phạm/rò rỉ dữ liệu (truy cập trái phép)
vocabulary.example: As we share more online, the risk of a massive data breach grows exponentially.
vocabulary.memory_hook: breach = lỗ hổng/vi phạm → 'data breach' = lỗ hổng khiến dữ liệu bị lộ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hành vi bắt nạt người khác thông qua các phương tiện điện tử/mạng xã hội.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The anonymity of the internet frequently fuels **cyberbullying**, a pervasive issue affecting youth mental health.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
cyber (không gian mạng) + bullying (bắt nạt) → bắt nạt trên không gian mạng.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết liền *cyberbullying*; đây là hành vi bắt nạt lặp lại/đáng kể qua công nghệ, không phải mọi bất đồng trên mạng.
vocabulary.definition_en: the use of electronic communication to bully a person, typically by sending intimidating or threatening messages
vocabulary.definition_vi: bắt nạt qua mạng
vocabulary.example: The anonymity of the internet frequently fuels cyberbullying, a pervasive issue affecting youth mental health.
vocabulary.memory_hook: cyber (không gian mạng) + bullying (bắt nạt) → bắt nạt trên không gian mạng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tiên tiến, hiện đại nhất, đi đầu trong một lĩnh vực (đặc biệt là công nghệ).

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> This research facility is equipped with **cutting-edge** technology that is very expensive.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
edge (lưỡi dao) đang được "cut" (mài sắc) → luôn sắc bén, tiên tiến nhất.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Cutting-edge' là tính từ ghép, luôn có gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ: 'cutting-edge technology', không viết rời 'cutting edge technology'.
vocabulary.definition_en: at the forefront of a field, especially technology; highly advanced and innovative
vocabulary.definition_vi: tiên tiến nhất, dẫn đầu công nghệ
vocabulary.example: This research facility is equipped with cutting-edge technology that is very expensive.
vocabulary.memory_hook: edge (lưỡi dao) đang được 'cut' (mài sắc) → luôn sắc bén, tiên tiến nhất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Lỗi thời, không còn được sản xuất hay sử dụng vì đã có cái mới thay thế.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many manual jobs are at risk of becoming **obsolete** due to the rise of AI.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"ob-" (ra khỏi) + liên tưởng "sold" (đã bán hết chỗ cho cái mới) → trở nên lỗi thời.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Obsolete' (đã lỗi thời) khác với 'obsolescent' (đang dần lỗi thời) — chú ý sắc thái mức độ.
vocabulary.definition_en: no longer produced or used; out of date and typically replaced by something newer
vocabulary.definition_vi: lỗi thời, không còn dùng nữa
vocabulary.example: Many manual jobs are at risk of becoming obsolete due to the rise of AI.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'ob-' (ra khỏi) + gợi liên tưởng 'solete' ~ 'solid/sold' → đã 'bán hết chỗ' cho cái mới, thành lỗi thời.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trí tuệ nhân tạo — lý thuyết và công nghệ giúp máy tính thực hiện các tác vụ vốn cần trí tuệ con người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Artificial intelligence** is a major and rapidly growing field of computer science.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
artificial (nhân tạo) + intelligence (trí tuệ) → trí tuệ do con người tạo ra.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết tắt chuẩn là 'AI' (in hoa), không phải 'A.I' có dấu chấm giữa; 'intelligence' không thêm 's' dù mang nghĩa khái quát.
vocabulary.definition_en: the theory and development of computer systems able to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence
vocabulary.definition_vi: trí tuệ nhân tạo
vocabulary.example: Artificial intelligence is a major and rapidly growing field of computer science.
vocabulary.memory_hook: artificial (nhân tạo) + intelligence (trí tuệ) → trí tuệ do con người tạo ra.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự giám sát liên tục và có hệ thống đối với một cá nhân hay nhóm người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Pervasive digital **surveillance** has raised profound concerns about personal privacy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
sur- (bên trên) + veiller (tiếng Pháp: canh gác) → nhìn từ trên xuống để canh chừng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Surveillance' luôn viết với 'ei' (không phải 'ai'); phát âm nhấn ở âm tiết cuối /veɪ/.
vocabulary.definition_en: close and continuous observation of a person or group, especially by an authority or system
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự giám sát (liên tục, có hệ thống)
vocabulary.example: Pervasive digital surveillance has raised profound concerns about personal privacy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: sur- (trên/bên trên) + veiller (tiếng Pháp: canh gác) → nhìn từ trên xuống để canh chừng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiện diện ở khắp mọi nơi cùng một lúc, phổ biến rộng rãi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Smartphones have become so **ubiquitous** as to be virtually indispensable to modern life.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
liên tưởng "ubiquitous" ~ "you-be-quick-to-us" → nó xuất hiện nhanh khắp mọi nơi bên ta.
vocabulary.common_error: Phát âm dễ sai: /juːˈbɪk.wə.təs/, không phải /ˈuː.bɪ.kwɪ.təs/; nhấn ở âm tiết thứ hai.
vocabulary.definition_en: present, appearing, or found everywhere at the same time
vocabulary.definition_vi: hiện diện khắp nơi, phổ biến ở mọi nơi
vocabulary.example: Smartphones have become so ubiquitous as to be virtually indispensable to modern life.
vocabulary.memory_hook: liên tưởng 'ubiquitous' ~ 'you-be-quick-to-us' → nó xuất hiện nhanh khắp mọi nơi bên ta.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thông tin sai lệch được lan truyền một cách có chủ đích nhằm đánh lừa người khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The unchecked dissemination of **disinformation** can rapidly erode public trust.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
dis- (sai/ngược) + information (thông tin) → thông tin bị bóp méo có chủ đích.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'disinformation' (sai lệch CÓ CHỦ Ý) với 'misinformation' (sai lệch do vô ý, không cố tình lừa dối).
vocabulary.definition_en: false information that is deliberately spread in order to deceive people
vocabulary.definition_vi: thông tin sai lệch có chủ đích (nhằm đánh lừa)
vocabulary.example: The unchecked dissemination of disinformation can rapidly erode public trust.
vocabulary.memory_hook: dis- (sai/ngược) + information (thông tin) → thông tin bị bóp méo có chủ đích.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình trạng không bị nhận diện danh tính, sự ẩn danh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The **anonymity** of the internet frequently fuels cyberbullying, a pervasive issue affecting youth mental health.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
an- (không) + onym (tên, gốc Hy Lạp) → không có tên → ẩn danh.
vocabulary.common_error: Danh từ là 'anonymity' /ˌæn.əˈnɪm.ə.ti/ (trọng âm rơi vào 'nym'), khác cách nhấn với tính từ 'anonymous' /əˈnɒn.ɪ.məs/.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of not being identified by name; the condition of being anonymous
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự ẩn danh
vocabulary.example: The anonymity of the internet frequently fuels cyberbullying, a pervasive issue affecting youth mental health.
vocabulary.memory_hook: an- (không) + onym (tên, gốc Hy Lạp 'onoma') → không có tên → ẩn danh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá trình chuyển đổi dữ liệu thành mã để ngăn truy cập trái phép.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> End-to-end **encryption** ensures that only the sender and recipient can read the contents of a message.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
en- (biến thành) + crypt (ẩn giấu, gốc Hy Lạp "kryptos") → biến thành dạng ẩn giấu.
vocabulary.common_error: Động từ là 'encrypt', danh từ là 'encryption'; đối lập với quá trình giải mã là 'decryption', không phải 'unencryption'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of converting information or data into a code, especially to prevent unauthorised access
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự mã hoá (dữ liệu)
vocabulary.example: End-to-end encryption ensures that only the sender and recipient can read the contents of a message.
vocabulary.memory_hook: en- (biến thành) + crypt (mật mã, gốc Hy Lạp 'kryptos' = ẩn giấu) → biến thành dạng ẩn giấu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trạng thái phải dựa vào hoặc bị chi phối bởi thứ gì đó khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> An over-**dependence** on digital devices risks eroding the art of face-to-face communication.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
de- (từ) + pend (treo, gốc Latin "pendere") → bị treo lơ lửng, dựa vào cái khác.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Dependence' (danh từ trừu tượng, sự phụ thuộc) khác 'dependent' (tính từ/danh từ chỉ người phụ thuộc); giới từ đi kèm là 'on', không phải 'to'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of relying on or being controlled by something or someone else
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự phụ thuộc
vocabulary.example: An over-dependence on digital devices risks eroding the art of face-to-face communication.
vocabulary.memory_hook: de- (từ) + pend (treo, gốc Latin 'pendere') → bị treo lơ lửng, dựa vào cái khác → phụ thuộc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khoảng cách giữa nhóm người có và không có khả năng tiếp cận công nghệ số.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The persistent **digital divide** continues to disadvantage marginalised communities.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
digital (số hoá) + divide (chia cắt) → công nghệ chia xã hội thành hai nhóm cách biệt.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Digital divide' là cụm danh từ cố định, không chia số nhiều thành 'digital divides' trừ khi nói cụ thể về nhiều loại khoảng cách (access, skills, outcomes divides).
vocabulary.definition_en: the gap between people who have easy access to digital technology and those who do not
vocabulary.definition_vi: khoảng cách số (giữa nhóm có và không có tiếp cận công nghệ)
vocabulary.example: The persistent digital divide continues to disadvantage marginalised communities.
vocabulary.memory_hook: digital (số hoá) + divide (chia cắt) → công nghệ chia xã hội thành hai nhóm cách biệt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cảnh sát dự đoán, việc dùng thuật toán dựa trên dữ liệu để dự báo nơi tội phạm có khả năng xảy ra.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Decisions once entrusted to civil servants — welfare eligibility, **predictive policing**, child-protection risk scoring — are increasingly delegated to opaque models.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
predictive (mang tính dự đoán) + policing (công tác cảnh sát) → dùng dữ liệu để đoán trước tội phạm sẽ xảy ra ở đâu.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Predictive policing' là cụm danh từ không đếm được chỉ một PHƯƠNG PHÁP, không phải tên gọi một cơ quan cụ thể; tránh viết hoa như danh từ riêng.
vocabulary.definition_en: the use of data-driven algorithms to forecast where crimes are likely to occur or who is likely to commit them
vocabulary.definition_vi: cảnh sát dự đoán (dùng thuật toán dữ liệu để dự báo tội phạm)
vocabulary.example: Decisions once entrusted to civil servants — welfare eligibility, predictive policing, child-protection risk scoring — are increasingly delegated to opaque models.
vocabulary.memory_hook: predictive (mang tính dự đoán) + policing (công tác cảnh sát) → dùng dữ liệu để đoán trước tội phạm sẽ xảy ra ở đâu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Môi trường (thường trên mạng) chỉ lặp lại những quan điểm giống với niềm tin sẵn có của một người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Social media algorithms create an **echo chamber** where you only hear agreeing opinions.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
echo (tiếng vọng) trong một chamber (căn phòng kín) → âm thanh chỉ dội lại chính nó, không có ý kiến mới.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *an echo chamber* cho môi trường củng cố cùng quan điểm; không nhầm với *filter bubble*, vốn nhấn mạnh cơ chế lọc cá nhân hóa.
vocabulary.definition_en: an environment, especially online, in which a person only encounters opinions that reinforce their own existing beliefs
vocabulary.definition_vi: buồng vọng âm (môi trường chỉ nghe thấy quan điểm giống mình)
vocabulary.example: Social media algorithms create an echo chamber where you only hear agreeing opinions.
vocabulary.memory_hook: echo (tiếng vọng) trong một chamber (căn phòng kín) → âm thanh chỉ dội lại chính nó, không có ý kiến mới.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Am hiểu và sử dụng thành thạo công nghệ hiện đại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> My grandfather is surprisingly **tech-savvy**; he uses his tablet and smartphone every day.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"savvy" (tiếng lóng: sành sỏi, hiểu biết) + tech → sành sỏi về công nghệ.
vocabulary.common_error: Cần dấu gạch nối *tech-savvy* khi làm tính từ; không viết *technology savvy* trong cách dùng thông thường.
vocabulary.definition_en: having a good understanding of and skill in using modern technology
vocabulary.definition_vi: am hiểu và thành thạo công nghệ
vocabulary.example: My grandfather is surprisingly tech-savvy; he uses his tablet and smartphone every day.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'savvy' (tiếng lóng: sành sỏi, hiểu biết) + tech → sành sỏi về công nghệ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Dán mắt vào màn hình, không thể rời mắt khỏi thiết bị điện tử.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Teenagers nowadays spend hours **glued to the screen**, completely ignoring their surroundings.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
glue (keo dán) → mắt như bị dán chặt vào màn hình, không rời được.
vocabulary.common_error: Cấu trúc bị động 'be/remain/stay glued to sth', không dùng 'glue to' ở dạng chủ động khi mô tả người xem.
vocabulary.definition_en: unable or unwilling to stop looking at a screen; completely absorbed in it
vocabulary.definition_vi: dán mắt vào màn hình (không rời mắt)
vocabulary.example: Teenagers nowadays spend hours glued to the screen, completely ignoring their surroundings.
vocabulary.memory_hook: glue (keo dán) → mắt như bị dán chặt vào màn hình, không rời được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tụt hậu, không bắt kịp những xu hướng hoặc phát triển mới nhất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> If your business doesn't have a website or social media presence, you are seriously **behind the curve**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
curve (đường cong tăng trưởng) → đứng phía sau đường cong nghĩa là chưa bắt kịp xu hướng.
vocabulary.common_error: Đối lập với 'behind the curve' là 'ahead of the curve' (đi trước xu hướng), không phải 'in front of the curve'.
vocabulary.definition_en: failing to keep up with current developments or trends, especially in technology or business
vocabulary.definition_vi: tụt hậu, chậm bắt kịp xu hướng
vocabulary.example: If your business doesn't have a website or social media presence, you are seriously behind the curve.
vocabulary.memory_hook: curve (đường cong tăng trưởng) → đứng phía sau đường cong nghĩa là chưa bắt kịp xu hướng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đột ngột ngừng hỗ trợ hoặc cấp vốn cho một dự án, khiến nó phải dừng lại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> After losing millions of dollars, the investors finally decided to **pull the plug** on the failing software project.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
pull (rút) + plug (phích cắm) → rút phích điện → khiến mọi thứ ngừng hoạt động hoàn toàn.
collocations: pull the plug on a project
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn cần giới từ 'on' khi nêu đối tượng bị dừng: 'pull the plug ON sth', không phải 'pull the plug of/for sth'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to suddenly stop supporting or funding a project or activity, causing it to end
vocabulary.definition_vi: rút phích cắm, ngừng cấp vốn/chấm dứt (một dự án)
vocabulary.example: After losing millions of dollars, the investors finally decided to pull the plug on the failing software project.
vocabulary.memory_hook: pull (rút) + plug (phích cắm) → rút phích điện → khiến mọi thứ ngừng hoạt động hoàn toàn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Việc dùng thuật toán tự động để đưa ra hoặc thực thi các quyết định, thay vì con người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Algorithmic governance**, it transpires, is governance by another name — and it must answer to due process.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
algorithm (thuật toán) + governance (quản trị) → để máy tính ra quyết định thay con người.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Governance' (sự quản trị, hệ thống điều hành) khác 'government' (chính phủ, một tổ chức cụ thể) — không dùng thay thế cho nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: the practice of using automated algorithms, rather than human officials, to make or enforce rules and decisions
vocabulary.definition_vi: quản trị bằng thuật toán (ra quyết định tự động thay vì con người)
vocabulary.example: Algorithmic governance, it transpires, is governance by another name — and it must answer to due process.
vocabulary.memory_hook: algorithm (thuật toán) + governance (quản trị) → để máy tính ra quyết định thay con người.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Người hoặc tổ chức kiểm soát quyền tiếp cận vào một nguồn thông tin hay cơ hội.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The European Union's Digital Markets Act designates dominant platforms as '**gatekeepers**' and mandates interoperability.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
gate (cổng) + keeper (người giữ) → người đứng canh cổng, quyết định ai được đi qua.
vocabulary.common_error: *Gatekeeper* là người/tổ chức kiểm soát quyền tiếp cận; không nhầm với *gateway*, tức cổng hoặc phương tiện truy cập.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person or organisation that controls access to something, especially information or opportunities
vocabulary.definition_vi: người/tổ chức kiểm soát cửa ngõ tiếp cận (thông tin, thị trường)
vocabulary.example: The European Union's Digital Markets Act designates dominant platforms as 'gatekeepers' and mandates interoperability.
vocabulary.memory_hook: gate (cổng) + keeper (người giữ) → người đứng canh cổng, quyết định ai được đi qua.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bỏ qua một giai đoạn phát triển trung gian để nhảy vọt thẳng lên trình độ cao hơn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Mobile penetration has allowed emerging economies to **leapfrog** legacy infrastructure entirely.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
leap (nhảy) + frog (con ếch) → như trò chơi nhảy cóc, bỏ qua hẳn một bước để tiến thẳng lên.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *leapfrog a stage/competitor* hoặc *leapfrog into something*; không thêm *over* khi đã có tân ngữ trực tiếp trong mẫu này.
vocabulary.definition_en: to bypass an intermediate stage of development by jumping directly to a more advanced one
vocabulary.definition_vi: nhảy vọt, bỏ qua giai đoạn phát triển trung gian
vocabulary.example: Mobile penetration has allowed emerging economies to leapfrog legacy infrastructure entirely.
vocabulary.memory_hook: leap (nhảy) + frog (con ếch) → như trò chơi nhảy cóc, bỏ qua hẳn một bước để tiến thẳng lên.
